opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, in 2024 the landscape was pretty homogeneous. Most of the open-source models people cared about were essentially variants of the Llama architecture: a decoder-only transformer, RMSNorm, rotary position embeddings, SwiGLU in the MLP, and either standard multi-head attention or grouped-query attention. When a new model came out, it was usually a Llama with a few tweaks. Maybe a different normalization placement, a slightly different RoPE scaling, a bias term here or there.

So for an inference engine like vLLM, adding a new model was mostly a matter of writing a model file that reused the same building blocks we already had: the same attention backend, the same paged KV cache, the same fused kernels for linear layers and activations. A lot of the time a contributor from the model vendor could do it in a day or two, sometimes just by copying the Llama implementation and changing a few lines. The core of the engine, meaning scheduling, memory management, and the attention kernels, didn't need to change at all.

Also, the models were mostly dense. You didn't have to think much about expert parallelism, load balancing across experts, or exotic attention variants. Tensor parallelism worked in a fairly standard way, and the KV cache had a uniform shape across all layers, which made paged attention very clean.

Things got a lot more complicated after that. DeepSeek brought in MLA, which changes what you actually cache, plus large-scale MoE. Then you got hybrid models mixing full attention with sliding window or linear attention and state-space layers, so different layers need different cache layouts. Then multimodal inputs, much longer contexts, new quantization formats, and so on. Each of those touches the core of the engine, not just the model definition. Looking back, 2024 was kind of a golden period where "supporting a model" mostly meant describing it, not re-engineering the system around it.

r001.rationale: The response attributes ease to architectural similarity and reuse of existing engine components, but it does not connect that ease to limited model–hardware coupling.

r002.rationale: It identifies MLA and hybrid attention variants as changes that affect caching and require changes to the inference engine’s core.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was mostly a matter of how homogeneous the architecture landscape had become. Almost every open-source model released in 2024 was a dense decoder-only Transformer, and the differences between them were small: a different normalization layer, a slightly different attention variant, a different activation in the MLP, maybe a tweak to positional encoding. Once vLLM had a solid implementation of LLaMA, supporting a new model was often just copying that file and changing a handful of lines. We used to joke that the "LLaMA-like" family covered 90% of what came out.

The other piece is that the whole ecosystem had converged on a common interface. Hugging Face set the de facto standard for how weights are stored, how configs are written, how tokenizers behave. So when a lab released a model, the checkpoint format and config were already in a shape we understood, and we didn't have to reverse-engineer anything. The model teams themselves also increasingly wanted day-zero support in inference engines, so they would reach out before release, send us the architecture details, and sometimes even submit the PR themselves.

So in 2024 the hard problems were really on the systems side: scheduling, memory management, quantization, kernels. Adding a model was not where the difficulty was. That changed later as architectures started diverging again, with things like MoE at large scale, hybrid attention, multimodal encoders, and so on. But for most of 2024, model support felt almost routine.

r001.rationale: The response attributes ease to similar model architectures and converging formats, but does not identify limited coupling between models and hardware as a reason.

r002.rationale: It mentions attention variants and later hybrid attention, but does not say that more complex attention algorithms could substantially affect inference engines.

astra-6.text: The main reason was that most open-source models shared very similar architectures. They were largely decoder-only Transformers, often quite close to Llama. So once an inference engine supported that basic architecture, adding another model usually meant adapting a few details—how the weights were named and loaded, the attention configuration, or the positional embeddings. You could reuse most of the execution code and optimized kernels. There were exceptions, but for many models, you weren’t implementing a new architecture from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response attributes ease to models sharing similar decoder-only Transformer architectures and reusable code, not to limited coupling between models and hardware.

r002.rationale: It mentions attention configuration as a detail to adapt, but does not identify more complex attention algorithms as an exception that could substantially affect inference engines.

sol-6.1.text: In 2024, most open-source models had very similar architectures. They were largely variations on the same Transformer design, so an inference engine already had most of the building blocks. Supporting a new model often meant adapting how the weights were loaded and handling a few architectural differences, rather than implementing a whole new set of operators. That made adding model support relatively straightforward.

r001.rationale: The response attributes ease to similar Transformer architectures and reusable engine components. It does not mention limited coupling between models and hardware.

r002.rationale: The response mentions architectural differences generally but does not identify more complex attention algorithms as an exception or discuss their effect on inference engines.
